activities.anchor: some celebrated successes did it the other way round
activities.caption: growth or development — drag the divider
activities.name: devGrowthCompare

config.prompt: The field's opening distinction — drag between the two:

before.label: Economic growth
before.text: More output year on year, counted as GDP rising — a quantity. A country can grow for decades while its people die young, if the gains sit in an enclave around oil wells or mines.

after.label: Development
after.text: A transformation in how people live — Costa Rica, Kerala and Sri Lanka reached long, literate, healthy lives on modest incomes, through deliberate public health and schooling.

config.why: A quantity versus a change in kind — the two can move in opposite directions, which is why this field counts lives, not only output.

activities.anchor: The world economy, it argued, is wired together
activities.caption: pair each theory with its claim
activities.name: devTheoryMatch

config.prompt: Four answers to 'how does development happen?' — pair each with its claim:

pairs.right: one ladder every country climbs, from traditional society to mass consumption
a rich core buys cheap raw materials and sells back dear manufactures — underdevelopment is made
development is the expansion of what people can be and do
present needs, without compromising future generations

config.why: Each answer reframes the goal or the mechanism — and the field now asks which institutions and histories separate the countries that converged from those that did not.

activities.anchor: It earns its centrality by being countable and comparable
activities.caption: find the faulty line — GDP's definition, read closely
activities.name: devGdpSpot

config.prompt: One of these readings of GDP's definition is backwards — click it:
lines: GDP = the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a period.
Unpaid care work is counted, because it is economically valuable.
Cutting a forest counts as income; the loss of the forest counts as nothing.
The per-capita mean says nothing about who beneath it holds the money.
Comparing countries honestly needs PPP — a dollar buys far more haircuts in Lagos than in London.
config.correction: Backwards — market value means anything without a price vanishes: unpaid care work and the informal economy never appear, and much of that work is done by women.
config.why: Every word of the definition is also a limitation — market value, produced, per capita, and the PPP adjustment each hide something.

config.prompt: From three dimensions to one score — put the construction in order:
items: Measure a long life — life expectancy at birth
Measure knowledge — mean and expected years of schooling
Measure a decent standard of living — PPP-adjusted income per person
Combine the three as a geometric mean, scored between 0 and 1
Read it against income: who lands above what their income predicts, who below?
config.why: The geometric mean punishes a very low score in any one dimension — so a country cannot buy its way to a high HDI with money alone.

config.prompt: The World Bank's international extreme poverty line (2021 PPP) — place it on the dollars-per-day scale.
config.why: About 3 US dollars per person per day at 2021 purchasing-power parity — subsistence itself; national poverty lines capture what each society considers minimally decent.

activities.anchor: bends away from a perfectly flat line
activities.caption: which Lorenz curve is the unequal one?
activities.name: devLorenzTrace

config.prompt: In one country the poorest half of the population holds only a small fraction of income; in another it holds half. Which curve is the unequal one?

curves.label: B: a gentle bow below the line
C: a deep bow below the line

config.why: The further the Lorenz curve bows below the equality line, the higher the Gini: Nordics in the high 20s, the US near 40, South Africa and Brazil in the 50s and beyond.

activities.anchor: rural girls versus urban boys is the classic
activities.caption: true or false — averages and the people they hide
activities.name: devDisaggJudge

statements.s: Two countries with identical GDP per capita can differ wildly in who is poor.
statements.why: That difference is precisely the development question: which institutions convert income into widespread capability, and which into enclaves.

statements.s: A country on track for its aggregate goal cannot contain populations decades behind it.
statements.why: Disaggregation by gender, region, ethnicity and age routinely reveals exactly that — one persistent slice trails every national headline.

statements.s: City dwellers in Shanghai live much like the average Italian.
statements.why: The contrasts inside one country can be that stark — while many rural Chinese live closer to the average person in Sub-Saharan Africa.

statements.s: Because income distributions are skewed, most people earn less than the mean income.
statements.why: A few very high earners pull the mean upward — which is why careful statistics prefer the median, the person halfway up the queue.

config.prompt: Small-loan platforms serving people excluded from ordinary banks publish striking figures — near what share of their loans is paid back?
config.why: Near 97 percent, even among the poorest borrowers — repayment that high, without collateral, is the surprise that made the model famous.
config.context: What was missing was not effort but the freedom to borrow.
